programme: MECP2-mediated chromatin repression of a stress/apoptosis-linked target set (including ESR1, TFF1, IGFBP3, ALOX5, CCND1 on one side and BDNF, NOX4, GAD1, RELN, FKBP5 on the other) — a single strong node rather than a multi-factor complex; none of the other eleven concordant factors (PML, GTF3A, ID4, ZNF24, IKZF3, CDX1, MYCN, ZNF135, FOXN1, CDX2, SALL1) has documented footing in both diseases and so cannot be added to the module without overreach.
role_in_a: In rectal cancer, MECP2 is reported as a transcription factor associated with metastatic progression of colorectal cancer, consistent with repression/derepression of proliferation- and hormone-responsive targets in its set (ESR1, TFF1, IGFBP3, CCND1).
role_in_b: In stroke, MECP2 is a downstream target of microRNA-132 whose de-repression after ischemia-reperfusion drives neuronal apoptosis, plausibly acting through its neuronal/stress targets (BDNF, NOX4, GAD1, RELN).
shared_axis: Both roles are the same repressor engaging its stress/apoptosis-adjacent target network under injury, but the triggers are unrelated (tumor microenvironment versus ischemia-reperfusion) — this is the same regulatory node being pulled on twice, not a shared causal pathway between the two diseases.
reasoning: MECP2 is the only factor with independent, on-topic citations placing it in both Rectal_Cancer and Stroke, so the node itself is real; but nothing in the retrieved material connects the two placements to each other, and colorectal cancer and cerebral ischemia are not an anatomically or clinically obvious pairing. Because only one of the twelve concordant factors clears this bar, this reads as a narrow, single-node signal rather than a multi-factor programme, which caps confidence at moderate.
support: PMID 30546056 — places MECP2 in Rectal_Cancer as associated with colorectal cancer metastasis. PMID 41989510 — places MECP2 in Stroke, showing it mediates ischemia-reperfusion-induced neuronal apoptosis and is targeted by microRNA-132.
how_to_falsify: Knock down MECP2 in parallel in a rectal cancer model (organoid or xenograft, assaying invasion/metastatic markers) and in a cerebral ischemia-reperfusion model (e.g., MCAO mice, assaying infarct volume and neuronal apoptosis); if MECP2 loss changes neither phenotype as the cited papers would predict, or if ChIP-seq/CUT&RUN in the two tissue contexts shows no shared target engagement (ESR1/TFF1 axis versus BDNF/NOX4 axis), the shared-node account fails.
caveats: 60 patient-group comparisons across 6 independent cohort pairs, blood vs. colorectal tissue. MECP2 is concordant in 26/60 groups — moderate, not top-tier (PML at 34/60 and GTF3A at 33/60 recur more often but lack bidirectional documented placement, so recurrence rank and evidentiary strength diverge here). The tissue-generic exclusion list removed most of the immune/stress transcription factors (IRF1, STAT5A/B, FOS, JUNB, ETS1, IRF8, CEBPD, ID2, HLX, NFATC2, SPIB) that would otherwise be the default guess for a blood–colorectal shared axis, so this account cannot lean on generic inflammatory signaling. Single-view exclusions (KLF7, DNMT3L, ZNF410, etc.) rule out a story built on one subgroup. The PML stroke hits are a name confound with progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, not the gene, and were excluded from consideration accordingly. Most other factors (PML, CDX1, CDX2, FOXN1) have real support only in rectal cancer, with no stroke counterpart at all, so they were left out of the carrying set rather than stretched into it.
